blocks.text: His face had strong—very strong—features, sharp and curved like an eagle’s. The upper part of his thin nose was high, and his nostrils were unusually curved. He had a high, rounded forehead. Hair grew very thinly around his temples, at the sides of his forehead, but it grew thickly everywhere else. His eyebrows were very large and heavy, and they almost met above his nose. Their bushy hair seemed to curl because there was so much of it. As far as I could see it under his heavy moustache, his mouth was firmly set and looked rather cruel. He had unusually sharp white teeth, and they stuck out over his lips. Those lips were remarkably red, which showed surprising life and energy in a man of his age. As for the rest, his ears were pale and extremely pointed at the tops. His chin was wide and strong, and his cheeks were thin but firm. The overall impression was an extraordinary paleness.

Until now, I had noticed the backs of his hands as they rested on his knees in the light of the fire. They had seemed rather white and delicate. Now, seeing them close to me, I could not help noticing that they were rather rough. They were wide, with short, thick fingers. Strangely enough, there were hairs in the middle of the palm. His nails were long and thin, and they were cut to a sharp point. When the Count leaned over me and his hands touched me, I could not hold back a shudder. Perhaps his breath smelled foul, but a horrible sick feeling came over me. No matter what I did, I could not hide it. The Count clearly noticed this and pulled back. He gave a grim kind of smile. His teeth stuck out, and this smile showed them more than he had shown them until then. With that smile, he sat down again on his own side of the fireplace. We were both silent for a while. As I looked towards the window, I saw the first faint line of light from the coming dawn. There seemed to be a strange quiet over everything. But as I listened, I heard the howling of many wolves. It sounded as if it came from down below in the valley. The Count’s eyes shone brightly, and he said:
“Listen to them—the children of the night. What music they make!” He saw, I suppose, some expression on my face that was strange to him, and he added:
“Ah, sir, you people who live in the city cannot share the feelings of the hunter.” Then he stood up and said:

“But you must be tired. Your bedroom is all ready, and tomorrow you can sleep as late as you want. I have to be away until the afternoon, so sleep well and dream well!” With a polite bow, he opened the door to the eight-sided room for me himself, and I went into my bedroom....

I am deep in a sea of wonders. I have doubts. I am afraid. I think strange things that I do not dare to admit to my own soul. May God keep me safe, if only for the sake of the people who are dear to me!

7 May.—It is early morning again, but I have rested and enjoyed the last twenty-four hours. I slept until late in the day and woke up on my own. After I got dressed, I went into the room where we had eaten supper. I found a cold breakfast laid out. There was also coffee, kept hot because the pot had been put on the stone floor of the fireplace. There was a card on the table with these words written on it:

“I have to be away for a while. Do not wait for me.—D.” I started eating and enjoyed a large, satisfying meal. When I had finished, I looked for a bell to let the servants know I was done. However, I could not find one. There are certainly strange things missing in the house, considering the extraordinary signs of wealth around me. The dishes and serving pieces for the table are made of gold. They are so beautifully made that they must be worth a huge amount of money. The curtains and the cloth coverings on the chairs and sofas are made of the most expensive and beautiful materials. So are the curtains hanging around my bed. They must have been worth an almost unbelievable amount when they were made, because they are hundreds of years old, yet still in excellent condition. I saw something like them in Hampton Court. There, however, they were worn, coming apart into loose threads, and full of holes eaten by moths. But still, there is no mirror in any of the rooms. There is not even a small dressing mirror on my table. I had to get the little shaving mirror from my bag before I could either shave or brush my hair. I have not seen a servant anywhere yet, or heard any sound near the castle except the howling of wolves. I had my meal between five and six o’clock, so I do not know whether to call it breakfast or dinner. Some time after I finished it, I looked around for something to read. I did not want to go around the castle until I had asked the Count’s permission. There was nothing at all in the room—no book, no newspaper, and not even anything for writing. So I opened another door in the room and found a kind of library. I tried the door opposite mine, but I found it locked.
